ext.title: Pinpointing the Powerful: Co-voting Network Centrality as a Measure of Political Influence (Online Appendix)

ext.research_question: Can network centrality computed from co-voting records (correlations between members' voting records) identify the actual cue-provider or leader in a legislature, and in particular does a proposed absolute-value centrality measure separate cue-providers from followers and majoritarians where the traditional centrality approach cannot? (Inferred from the appendix; the main question is stated in the published article, which is not in this text.)
ext.theory: Leader or cue-provider theory: a leader whose followers vote with her some percentage of the time (ally followers, opponent followers, or others at other rates). The appendix argues the leader should have the highest network centrality in a co-voting network built from phi correlations of voting records (lines 318-353). Majoritarians are members who vote with the majority; the traditional centrality approach can rank majoritarians above the actual cue-provider (Figure 4 text, line 303).
ext.data: Empirical data (Table 1, line 12-120): 940 MEP observations (centrality N = 897 after network construction; left-right distance to EP median N = 868; pro/anti-EU distance to EP median N = 872). Unit is the MEP. Variables include centrality (mean .283, SD .138, range .006-.502), party leader (mean .05), committee leader (.09), EP leader (.03), coordinator (.23), reports drafted (mean 1.05), reports amended (6.73), opinions (.72), motions (6.82), speeches (29.07), questions (20.07), declarations (.58), tenure (1.58), party size (172.01), female (.30). Period of the European Parliament data is not stated in the appendix text. Simulated data (Figures 1-6, lines 289-313): 1000 simulated networks per network class (simple, moderate, complex); 1000 simulations; 100 legislators; 1000 rounds of voting in the Figure 5 runs. Figure 6 uses three parameterizations: US (1 cue-provider, 1 majoritarian, 40 allies, 40 opponents, 20 others at 50%), Supermajority (1 cue-provider, 1 majoritarian, 67 allies, 33 opponents), and EP (1 cue-provider, 1 majoritarian, 37 allies, 25 opponents, 38 others at varied rates, roughly the seven-party EP seat allotment).
ext.method: Centrality is built from pairwise phi correlations of binary voting records (Table 1 is the 2x2 contingency table underlying phi, lines 331-341). The appendix uses an absolute-value version of this centrality, referred to as the "posterior" measure, which is compared with the traditional (signed) centrality calculation. Analytic method: Hypothesis 1 (leader centrality >= follower centrality) is proved algebraically for a three-voter legislature (leader plus two followers) with follow probabilities q2 and q3 and leader Yes-probability p; the condition reduces to q2 < 1 and q3 < 1 (lines 319-345). The result is extended to n voters by a term-by-term comparison, arguing that each phi term depends only on p and the relevant follow probabilities, so it is unchanged as voters are added (lines 347-353). Simulation method: Monte Carlo generation of cueing networks in three complexity classes, computing the posterior centrality from simulated voting records and correlating it with betweenness, closeness, and weighted degree (Figure 5); and t-tests of cue-provider centrality against the maximum follower and a majoritarian across rounds of voting (Figure 6). Figures 1-4 show cue-provider centrality as a function of follow probabilities.
ext.scope: Population: members of the European Parliament (party groups named in Table 2: EPP, EPP-ED, PES, ALDE, G/EFA, EUL/NGL, IND/DEM, UEN), plus stylized simulated legislatures (US, supermajority, and EP-style). Institution: European Parliament (empirical) and abstract legislatures (theory). Era: not stated in the appendix text. The theoretical result is stated for single-party legislatures under the stated assumptions.

key_findings.finding: Under the assumptions, in a three-voter legislature the leader's centrality is greater than or equal to each follower's centrality; the condition reduces to q2 < 1 and q3 < 1, which hold by inspection.
key_findings.location: Complete Proof of Leader Centrality, Hypothesis 1 proof (lines 318-345)
key_findings.numbers: Conditions: q2 < 1 and q3 < 1 (follow probabilities are probabilities).

key_findings.finding: The three-voter result is extended to n voters for the single-party case: the cue-provider has greater or equal centrality than any follower regardless of exogenous parameter values. The text states 'greater' for n = 4 but the inequalities derived are weak (>=).
key_findings.numbers: Proof given for 3, 4, and arbitrary n voters.

key_findings.finding: Posterior absolute-value centrality recovers the true network centralities of simulated cueing networks; it is highly correlated with closeness and weighted degree even in complex networks, and only weakly correlated with betweenness.
key_findings.numbers: Betweenness correlation about 0.25; closeness and weighted degree described as 'highly correlated' (no coefficient reported); 1000 simulations, 100 legislators, 1000 rounds of voting; 1000 networks per class.

key_findings.finding: Simple networks are recovered most accurately; moderate and complex networks less so, because network structure is lost when networks are converted to voting data.

Cue-provider centrality is significantly higher than the maximum follower and the majoritarian; significance grows with the number of voting rounds, and is described as comparable to available EP data at 1,000 rounds.
key_findings.numbers: Three parameterizations (US, Supermajority, EP); t-scores are described as significant but no t-values are given in the text.

key_findings.finding: With allies and opponents following at 65% and 35%, cue-provider centrality is clearly higher than majoritarians and followers across the 35%-65% range, though the gap is less pronounced than at 80%/20%.
key_findings.numbers: Parameterization 65%/35% versus 80%/20% in the published article.

key_findings.finding: With allies at 80% and opponents at 35%, the absolute-value centrality yields systematically higher cue-provider centrality, while the traditional approach cannot distinguish the cue-providers.
With a third group following at 35%, the traditional calculation makes majoritarians systematically more central than the actual cue-provider; the absolute-value measure corrects this.
Cue-provider centrality is maximized when follow probabilities approach 0 or 1 and minimized when both are 50%.
key_findings.numbers: Follow probabilities on the x and y axes; minimum at (50%, 50%).

key_findings.finding: Descriptive: the top-ranked MEP overall is Braghetto (EPP) at centrality 0.5019; the top 17 are from the EPP; the 18th is Sakalas (PES) at 0.475. Group leaders: PES Sakalas 0.475; ALDE Duff 0.4441; G/EFA Onesta 0.2046; EUL/NGL Svensson 0.1737; IND/DEM Wojciechowski 0.3248; UEN Masiel 0.3893.
key_findings.numbers: Overall mean centrality .283 (Table 1); EPP-ED block lists 5 ranks with the second entry labelled '5' (apparent labeling error in the table, lines 157-171).

limitations: Results are described as highly dependent on parameterization; three sample parameterizations are used (lines 309).
Betweenness centrality correlates only about 0.25 with the posterior measure, so the measure does not recover betweenness well (line 308).
Moderate and complex cueing networks lose network structure when converted to voting data, reducing recovery accuracy (line 308).
The proof gives weak inequalities (greater than or equal to), not strict inequalities, although the n-voter text concludes 'greater' (lines 344-353).
The proof is restricted to a single-party legislature and to the stated assumptions (independent follow probabilities, fixed p); multi-party extensions are not proved here (line 352).
No t-scores or correlation coefficients are reported for closeness and weighted degree; significance is asserted, not quantified (lines 308-309).
The empirical sample period, the Parliament term, and the construction of the co-voting network are not stated in this appendix text.
The appendix refers to a published article for the main figures and the 80%/20% parameterization, which is not in this text; claims beyond the appendix cannot be checked here.
Table 2 contains a rank-label error (the second EPP-ED entry is labelled '5').

short_quotes.quote: The results are highly dependent on parameterization

rel.summary_md:
This is the online appendix to Ringe and Wilson's paper on co-voting centrality. It holds a proof, simulations and descriptive tables from the European Parliament. The authors build a network from pairwise phi correlations of members' binary voting records. They score each member by an absolute-value (sign-blind) centrality: a member followed reliably by allies (positive phi) or reliably opposed by opponents (negative phi) both count toward that member's centrality.

**Proof.** For a single-party legislature, they show the leader's centrality is at least as high as any follower's. The condition reduces to q2 < 1 and q3 < 1. The inequalities are weak (greater than or equal), although the n-voter text says "greater".

**Simulations.** There were 1,000 networks per complexity class, with 100 legislators and 1,000 voting rounds.
- The absolute-value measure separates the cue-provider from followers and from "majoritarians" (members who usually vote with the majority).
- The traditional signed measure can rank majoritarians above the true cue-provider when a third group follows at 35% (Figure 4).
- The measure correlates highly with closeness and weighted degree (no coefficient reported), but only about 0.25 with betweenness.
- Moderate and complex networks lose structure when converted to voting data.
- The authors say the results are "highly dependent on parameterization".

**Empirical side.** The data cover 897 MEPs with centrality scores (mean .283). The parliamentary term is not stated in the appendix.

**Why it matters here.**
- Melange has one co-voting layer: the signed vote backbone in the Draft Systems R script, plus its party-controlled Option C. That layer found the raw signed backbone was about 95% party, then dropped the negative side. The paper offers a mechanism for the first finding (the signed measure rewards majoritarians) and an argument against the second (negative ties carry cue-provider information).
- The paper also clarifies the June 2026 retirement of cosponsor centrality from the Influence pillar. The paper treats sign-blindness as a property of a leadership measure, not as a flaw. That supports the system's two-axis rule, which keeps influence and alignment as separate axes.
- None of this transfers directly. The evidence is analytic and simulated, with European Parliament data, and it concerns co-voting, not cosponsorship.

bearings.paper_claim: Signed (traditional) co-voting centrality cannot separate the cue-provider from majoritarians, and with a third group following at 35% it ranks majoritarians above the true cue-provider. The absolute-value measure, which credits reliable negative correlation (opponents following at 20-35%) as well as positive correlation, corrects this. Cue-provider centrality is lowest when follow probabilities are 50% and highest as they approach 0 or 1.
bearings.paper_location: Figure 4 text (line 303); Figure 3 text (line 297); Figure 1 text (line 291)
bearings.system_side: The component text says DW-NOMINATE vote edges were rejected in favour of a signed backbone. The co-voting backbone is built by R backbone::sdsm(signed=TRUE) on a member x (vote, side) bipartite graph, so the projection counts agreements (yea-yea plus nay-nay). The brain records that the raw signed backbone was about 95% party (93% of positive edges same-party, 99% of negative edges cross-party). Option C used a party-controlled null and then DROPPED the negative side, keeping only cross-party positive edges as 'Vote Affinity' (a 30% booster in the Signed Coalitions sheet). Separately, the Python signed_coalitions.py partitions the signed MENTION layer (member_references.json), not votes.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper models cue-taking around a single leader in a single-party legislature, with simulated, independent follow probabilities and European Parliament data. Its target is leader identification, while the system's goal is cross-party affinity for flip targeting, so the critique of dropping negatives applies only if the layer were reused for leadership or cue detection. The paper's majoritarian mechanism plausibly explains why the raw signed backbone collapsed onto party in a two-party House. That explanation is UNVERIFIED for US data and the 119th Congress until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Sign-blind (absolute-value) centrality is the construct that identifies leaders and cue-providers. The leader's centrality is >= every follower's, given only q2 < 1 and q3 < 1, so direction-blindness is a design property of a leadership measure, not a defect. The posterior measure tracks closeness and weighted degree closely but correlates only about 0.25 with betweenness.
bearings.paper_location: Complete Proof of Leader Centrality (lines 318-345); Figure 5 text (line 308)
bearings.system_side: InfluenceScore = 0.60 x weighted out-degree + 0.25 x betweenness + 0.15 x eigenvector on the cosponsor network. It was retired from Influence on 2026-06-25 (AB13 0.65 -> 0) as 'direction-blind' because it raised anti-CU bill authors (Durbin, centrality 0.94, fell from rank 386 to 524 after removal). The live Influence pillar is committee-only. The system's stated rule is that rank measures influence and that stance is a separate axis.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's evidence concerns co-voting phi networks in the European Parliament plus simulations, not US cosponsorship. It suggests the retirement rationale mixed the two axes: a sign-blind leadership score is legitimate on the influence axis. However, the paper never validates centrality against outcomes such as bill passage, and Sotoudeh's highlight ('not a strong indicator of bill passage') still stands. The paper also implies the 0.25 betweenness weight is the least recoverable term if the network were ever rebuilt from votes. Any revived centrality rank is a heuristic model output, never an access or influence probability (D-025).

bearings.paper_claim: Converting cueing networks into voting data loses network structure. Simple networks are recovered well, moderate and complex ones less so, and betweenness recovery is only about 0.25.
bearings.system_side: The cascade kernel takes edge weights from cosponsorship, with p(u->v) = x/(x+6) and partisan factors cpf_diffusion and cpf_pressure. It does not infer edges from roll-call co-voting. The saturation constant 6 is unestimated.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This bears on any future proposal to estimate cascade edges or the saturation constant from roll-call agreement. The paper's simulations say node-level centrality survives aggregation into voting data but path or edge structure does not, so co-voting is a weak source for edge-level kernel calibration. It is evidence from simulated legislatures with independent follow probabilities, not from US data.

gaps_exposed: No component computes a leadership or cue-provider score from roll-call co-voting. The roll-call ledger exists (fec/legislation/collect_official_rollcall_events.py), but nothing turns it into a co-voting network apart from the June workbook-era Draft Systems _vote_backbone.R affinity layer.

The vote-backbone affinity layer discards negative (reliable-opposition) ties. Per the paper these carry cue-provider information, so the system cannot tell a reliable cross-pressure leader from a maverick, a confound the brain itself records (the Massie/Gosar/Roy negatives).
Nothing tests whether the raw signed backbone's collapse onto party is a majoritarian artifact, as the paper's Figure 4 mechanism predicts, rather than true party cueing.

The centrality retirement was judged on CU alignment (opponents rising), not on any leadership or effectiveness criterion. No test checks whether sign-blind centrality predicts effectiveness (CEL LES, bill advancement) on the influence axis.
flags: The paper's title frames co-voting centrality as 'a measure of political influence'. If adopted, any centrality rank must be worded as a heuristic model output, never as closeness, access or an influence probability (D-025).

The paper does not argue for either REJECTED SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges, or per-edge volume normalization). Phi correlation is a per-pair standardized agreement on votes, not a reweighting of cosponsor edges, so it must not be cited as support for per-edge volume normalization.

The component description for melange-sna.signed-coalitions says 'signed backbone' (vote-based), but fec/network/signed_coalitions.py:6-8 partitions the signed mention layer (member_references.json). The vote backbone lives only in Draft Systems/_vote_backbone.R and the workbook. The component inventory conflates the two.

The empirical evidence comes from European Parliament MEPs (term not stated) and the rest is simulation. Any claim transferred to the US House or Senate is UNVERIFIED (DE-062). The proof gives weak inequalities only and is restricted to a single-party legislature.
The empirical leader ranking pools 897 MEPs across party groups. Table 2 gives within-group leaders, but the overall rank is UNSTRATIFIED across the party fault line (the top 17 are all EPP).
rel.paul_alignment: Paul has no annotation on this paper. His centrality-component position is that more research on forms of centrality is needed (Ardekani), that directionality matters (Haythornthwaite), and that eigenvector centrality is not a strong indicator of bill passage (Sotoudeh highlight). The paper partly cuts against reading 'direction-blind' as a defect: it argues that sign-blindness is what lets centrality find cue-providers, which fits the system's own influence-versus-alignment two-axis rule. It agrees with Paul's call for more centrality forms, offering co-voting absolute-value centrality as a candidate he has not considered. His notes are not stale. However, the system's June decision to keep only positive cross-party vote-backbone edges is a choice his notes never address, and this paper bears on it directly.

related.why: Both build member networks from roll-call agreement. Aref & Neal partition the signed vote network, while Ringe & Wilson score nodes by absolute-value phi centrality, and both treat negative ties as informative. The system's vote backbone was built on the Aref & Neal lineage.
This is the earlier signed co-voting coalition partition. It is the coalition-level counterpart of the paper's node-level cue-provider centrality on the same kind of data.

Sotoudeh tests cosponsorship-network centrality against bill passage and finds eigenvector centrality weak. Ringe & Wilson validate co-voting centrality only against simulated ground truth, so together they bound what centrality can and cannot show.
Both rest on cue-taking theory in legislatures. Box-Steffensmeier measures cues via Dear Colleague letters in Congress, while Ringe & Wilson infer the cue-provider from voting correlations.
Both are roll-call methods. NOMINATE scales ideology, while Ringe & Wilson extract leadership centrality from the same binary vote matrix. The system rejected DW-NOMINATE vote edges.

Both treat network centrality as pricing a legislator's influence. Battaglini & Patacchini derive Katz-Bonacich centrality theoretically (the system's kb_benchmark), while Ringe & Wilson give a co-voting measure that recovers degree and closeness well.
